extracted.intended_audience: comedy writers, sketch/television producers, comedy historians, SNL/Late Night fans
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and observed practices for creating, pitching, and producing televised sketch comedy (SNL, Late Night, Dana Carvey Show, TV Funhouse) drawn from Robert Smigel's interview and career examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of limitations/standards to sharpen comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: The bear bit being funnier due to the limitations put on it by Standards & Practices; getting notes from Standards & Practices to tweak sketches (e.g., 'Masturbating Bear', 'Conspiracy Theory Rock!').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constraints from censors, sponsors, or broadcast standards can force more inventive, funnier choices; treat imposed limits as creative fuel rather than only a restriction. Example: Masturbating Bear's funnier effect because of the limitations, and SNL tweaks requested by Standards & Practices for sketches skewering network parent companies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose medium to fit the comedic idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Turning to animation as a vehicle for comedy and wanting to be a cartoonist; creating animated pieces like 'Cluckin' Chicken' and 'TV Funhouse' that suited particular jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the format (animation, puppetry, live sketch, pre-taped remote) that best serves the joke's affordances — e.g., animation allows surreal visuals and parody of children's media; format choice can determine what jokes are possible and how they land.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance improvisation and pre-writing
rubrics_metrics.description: For 'Triumph the Insult Comic Dog' Smigel discusses how much is improvised and how much is written; some of the best lines were improvised and not pre-written.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberately mix scripted material with room for improvisation; design bits that allow performers to riff so that spontaneous lines can emerge without losing structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find the rhythm/music in an impression or piece
rubrics_metrics.description: Working with Dana Carvey on impressions involved 'finding the music' in an impression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search for cadence, rhythm, and musicality in impressions and sketches — matching timing and 'music' to the performer makes impressions more distinct and effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize individuality and originality of ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasis on the individuality of comedy ideas (examples: Jack Handey, Louis C.K.); 'individuality of comedy ideas' as a valued quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid recycling obvious premises; cultivate distinctive comedic voices and ideas that feel personal and singular rather than formulaic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use counterpoint/catharsis between character and host
rubrics_metrics.description: Triumph functions as catharsis for the audience because Conan is super polite and 'Triumph' is the opposite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create characters that provide contrast to the show's tone or host persona to produce comedic tension and catharsis (i.e., the comic disruptor vs. the polite host).

rubrics_metrics.name: Match performer style to format and audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Adam Sandler's style described as 'dry and conversational' that 'kills in read-through' but is 'hard to pull off in front of an audience.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When casting or tailoring material, consider whether a performer's style works better in a writers' room/read-through, pre-taped segment, or live performance; adapt staging and delivery to the strengths of the comedian.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advocate/persist to get risky material produced
rubrics_metrics.description: Smigel had to fight to get sketches aired (e.g., Gerald Ford sketch) and to have controversial material included; sketches sometimes only aired when particular hosts returned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to push and re-pitch material, especially edgier or unconventional bits; timing (which host is available) and persistence can be as important as quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody and intertextual reference as comedic affordances
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent parody of recognizable texts (Peanuts, Schoolhouse Rock, Batman, Disney vaults); using familiar cultural texts in animated sketches and parodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage audience familiarity with cultural artifacts to create humor through juxtaposition and subversion, while ensuring the parody adds a fresh angle rather than just copying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Play with provocative subtext and themes thoughtfully
rubrics_metrics.description: Working 'with ideas of homoeroticism and masculinity' in 'The Ambiguously Gay Duo' and related sketches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use subtext (sexuality, gender, politics) to add layers to jokes, but handle sensitive topics intentionally and with awareness of audience and context; subtext can deepen satire when done deliberately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive visual/technical devices can define a bit
rubrics_metrics.description: Clutch Cargo-style bits used a still photo with a real person's mouth; 'Fun with Real Audio' animated real audio clips between Larry King and Ross Perot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiment with unusual production techniques or visual devices that become the premise's gag — the technique itself can be the joke's engine and needs to be executed clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character design and physical props matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Details like Triumph's gold bow tie, cigar prop, and deadpan stare contributed to the character's persona.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use costume, props, and physical choices to quickly communicate character traits and comedic intent; small physical details can generate recurring jokes and recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assemble a writing/production team to achieve a specific tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Smigel describes putting together writing staffs (hiring Louis C.K., Dino Stamatopoulos, Stephen Colbert) to shape a show's voice and bits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curate writers and collaborators whose sensibilities align with the desired comedic direction; team composition influences which ideas surface and how they are refined.
